says: When the right-click menu is requested on the category tree it applies to the selected category; on the policy list it applies to the first selected row; with no selected row in the list the menu is not shown.
In the right-click menu, items meant only for policies are hidden when the target is a category, and items meant only for categories are hidden when the target is a policy.
Choosing All details on a category opens the category details; on a policy it opens the policy details.
Right-clicking a category in the tree selects that category first, so the menu acts on the one clicked.
A description is shown with each line stripped of leading and trailing spaces, and trailing blank space at the end of the whole text removed.
In the Open ADMX folder dialog the folder text box and Browse button are usable only while the custom folder choice is selected.

When the Open ADMX folder dialog appears, the custom folder choice is selected, and the domain definitions choice is offered only if the computer is in a domain and its shared definitions folder \\<domain>\SYSVOL\<domain>\Policies\PolicyDefinitions exists; otherwise it is disabled.

When the person confirms the Open ADMX folder dialog, the folder used is the Windows PolicyDefinitions folder for the local choice, the domain definitions folder for the domain choice, or the typed text for the custom choice.

When the chosen ADMX folder does not exist, the dialog stays open and the person is told "The folder you specified does not exist."; otherwise it closes accepted, carrying the choice to clear the existing workspace.
Choosing a POL file in the policy sources dialog offers only .pol files and does not warn when the chosen file already exists, so an existing or new file name can be picked.
In the policy sources dialog the computer registry text box is enabled only for the registry choice; the computer POL file name box and Browse button only for the POL file choice.

In the policy sources dialog the user registry box is enabled only for the registry choice, the POL file box and Browse only for the file choice, the SID box and Browse only for the per-user policy choice, and the hive path box and Browse only for the per-user hive choice.

When the policy sources dialog is accepted, the computer source is the local policy, the typed registry path, the typed POL file, or an empty scratch space, as chosen. If it cannot be created, the dialog stays open and the person is told "The computer policy loader could not be created. " followed by the reason.

When the policy sources dialog is accepted, the user source is the local policy, the typed registry path, the typed POL file, the per-user policy for a SID, the per-user hive file, or an empty scratch space, as chosen. If it cannot be created, the dialog stays open and the person is told "The user policy loader could not be created. " followed by the reason.
The section dialog is accepted only when User or Computer is selected, and reports that section; with neither selected, confirming does nothing.

When a user name is searched in the per-user policy dialog, it is translated to a SID shown in the SID box; if Windows cannot translate it the person is told "The name could not be translated to a SID."
When the per-user policy dialog is confirmed with a user name but no SID, the name is searched first; if that finds no SID the dialog stays open.

When the per-user policy dialog is confirmed with a SID that is not a valid SID, it stays open and the person is told "The SID is not valid. Enter a SID in the lower box, or enter a username in the top box and press Search to translate."; a valid SID is returned.
The per-user policy dialog clears both the user name and SID boxes each time it opens.
The user hive list shows each folder under C:\Users that holds an ntuser.dat file, skipping folders that are links (reparse points). Folders without an ntuser.dat are not listed.

Each listed user hive is marked Yes when it can be opened for reading and writing and the program runs as an administrator, No (unprivileged) when it opens but the program is not an administrator, No when access is denied, and No (in use) for any other failure to open it.
The user hive dialog is accepted only with a row selected, and returns C:\Users\<folder>\ntuser.dat for that row; with no row selected confirming does nothing.

A registry policy source accepts the root key names hkcu, hkey_current_user, hku, hkey_users, hklm and hkey_local_machine in any letter case; any other root is refused with "The root key is not valid." A path after the root is created if missing.

The local policy source uses the Machine or User Registry.pol under the Windows GroupPolicy folder and its gpt.ini; a per-user policy source uses GroupPolicyUsers\<SID>\User\Registry.pol and that folder's gpt.ini.
When a registry policy source is opened, the program writes and removes a test value under Software\Policies; the source is writable only if both succeed.

A user hive file is opened by turning on the backup and restore privileges and mounting it under a temporary name in the machine registry. If the mount does not produce a key, the source is read-only and is an empty scratch policy store.
A scratch space source starts as an empty policy store and is always writable.
An existing POL file is loaded, and is writable only if it can be opened for reading and writing; otherwise it can be viewed but not saved.
When the POL file does not exist, the program creates its folder and an empty POL file and the source is writable; every setting starts Not configured.
When the missing POL file or its folder cannot be created, the source is an empty unsaved policy store and is not writable.
Closing a mounted user hive source unloads the hive and reports success only if Windows unloads it; other source types report success without any step.

Saving the local policy source writes the POL file and raises the gpt.ini version. On Windows editions with Group Policy support it asks Windows to refresh policy and reports "saved to disk and invoked policy refresh".

Saving the local policy source on an edition without Group Policy support writes the POL file, applies only the changed values to the current registry, announces a settings change to all windows, and reports "saved to disk and applied diff to Registry".
Saving a POL file source writes the file only and reports "saved to disk"; no policy refresh is requested.
Saving a per-user policy source writes its POL file, raises its gpt.ini version and always requests a user policy refresh, reporting "saved to disk and invoked policy refresh".

Saving a registry source changes nothing and reports "already applied" because edits were live; a user hive source reports "will apply when policy source is closed"; scratch space reports "discarded".

Comments for a POL file or user hive source go in a .cmtx file beside it with the same name; a registry source uses Reg<User or Machine>.cmtx under the local application data Policy Plus folder; a local or per-user policy source uses comment.cmtx beside its Registry.pol; with no path there are no comments.
A registry source that could not be written offers no editing; any other source that is not writable allows editing but is not saved; scratch space is always writable.

Saving a policy source raises the gpt.ini Version by 65536 for a user source or by 1 for a machine source, adds Version=65537 if missing, and adds the machine and user Group Policy extension lines if missing. A missing gpt.ini is created with all three.
The status bar names a source as Local GPO, Registry, File, User GPO, User hive or Scratch space, followed by its path or argument in brackets when it has one.

A policy with a registry value counts toward Enabled when that value holds its on value (or the number 1 when none is defined), and toward Disabled when it holds its off value (or is queued for deletion when none is defined).
Each value in a policy's on value list counts toward Enabled, and each value in its off value list counts toward Disabled, when present.
For a list element, a key queued for deletion counts as one disabled element; if the key holds any values, it counts as one present element instead.
For a checkbox element queued for deletion counts as one disabled element; otherwise an off-value match counts as a tenth of a disabled element, and an on-value match counts as one present element.
For any other element, a value queued for deletion counts as one disabled element and a stored value counts as one present element.
Present elements count toward Enabled, and disabled elements are counted only if none are present.
A policy is Enabled when Enabled evidence exceeds Disabled evidence, Disabled when the reverse, Not configured when both are zero, and Unknown when both are equal and above zero.

A required number value is present only if the stored value is a whole number equal to it, a required text value only if stored text is equal to it, and a required deletion only if the value is queued for deletion.
A list of required values is present only when every value in it is present, each using its own key or the list's key.

Two policies in one category are merged into one for both user and computer when they share the same name, one is user and the other computer, they have the same explanation and the same registry key; one copy is removed.
A checkbox element reads as ticked when its on value is present, or its on value list is fully present, or, with neither defined, the stored number is 1; otherwise it reads as unticked.

An element reads as a list of entries: named entries if the person supplies names; else numbered values (name plus 1, 2, ... until one is missing) if it has a prefix; else every value name under the key.
A dropdown element reads as the first item whose value is present and whose value list, if any, is fully present; if none match, no item is selected.
Forgetting a policy removes every registry value it can affect (its own value, listed values, element values) from the source, and clears every value under each list element's key.

statement: Whether a policy save asks Windows to refresh or the program applies the change itself depends on a fixed list of Windows edition codes. Whether newer editions are on that list is assumed.

assumed.why: The list is a fixed set of numbers; which Windows editions they stand for is outside the code.
assumed.ifWrong: On an unlisted edition with Group Policy, saves would apply changes to the registry directly instead of refreshing policy.

evidence.shows: Edition code is tested against a fixed list of codes.

statement: Offering the domain definitions folder relies on Windows reporting the computer's domain. When Windows cannot, the choice is silently disabled, so domain-joined machines without reachable controllers cannot pick it.

assumed.why: The domain lookup is a framework call with no source here.
assumed.ifWrong: The domain choice could appear or stay disabled differently than described.

evidence.shows: Domain lookup failure is ignored and the domain choice disabled.

says: The section dialog has neither User nor Computer selected each time it opens.
The section dialog offers User and Computer only when the caller says each is available; an unavailable one is disabled.
